newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala peace talks will resume Saturday.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala peace talks will resume Saturday.

text.p: Peace talks between the Guatemalan government and leftist rebels, stalled for 12 days after a guerrilla commander was accused of kidnapping a woman, will resume on Saturday, the United Nations said on Friday.
Guatemala's 5-year-old peace process was interrupted on Oct. 28 after a rebel commander was arrested for holding a wealthy elderly woman for ransom.

After days of tense silence by the government and a series of olive branches offered by the rebel Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG), both sides said on Thursday they were ready to return to the negotiation table.

"The United Nations moderator has decided to convoke the delegations from both sides to renew the negotiation process on Nov. 9, 10 and 11," said a U.N. statement. The United Nations has been a go-between in the peace process since 1991.

President Alvaro Arzu told reporters on Friday he was confident Guatemala would have a final peace agreement before the end of the year, as planned before the recent crisis. He said negotiators would begin discussing a bilateral ceasefire rather than continuing talks on the post-war political role of the guerrillas, the topic on the table when talks broke off.
Guatemalans are anxious for an end to the 36-year armed conflict -- the last in Central America. More than 100,000 people, mostly civilians, have died and an estimated 40,000 are missing.

The talks, which had been running smoothly for months, were abruptly suspended after rebel commander Rafael Valdizon was arrested on suspicion of kidnapping a member of an influential family that owns Guatemala's only cement company.

Police briefly jailed Valdizon but let him go in return for the freeing of 86-year-old Olga Alvarado de Novella, whose whereabouts were still unknown to authorities. Police are searching for Valdizon and Arzu promised the rebel leader would be prosecuted if he is rearrested.
The URNG has often kidnapped people for ransom to finance its insurrection but pledged to end such practices under preliminary agreements reached with the government.

After the government charged the guerrilla with violating terms of the negotiations and suspended talks, the URNG high command made a series of conciliatory gestures. They condemned the kidnapping and a few days later announced they would suspend propaganda exercises by guerrillas in Guatemala.

But the government did not respond until rebel commander Rodrigo Asturias (alias Commander Gaspar Ilom), Valdizon's direct leader in one of the four factions that make up the URNG, announced on Thursday he would withdraw from the talks.
